title: Dark Venture: Battle of the Ancients - Narrative skirmish battles in a weird and twisted world
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FEqKnaBExZU

Five things, after real play. Daniel (@dungeondive) has now run two narrative scenarios, the cooperative adventure mode, a random "Will of the Ancients" variant and a straight competitive victory game — and still declines to call this a review.

The tour covers adventure mode, playing the Dargon against the Bomark and the Alder King. The Dargon gather resources, spend them on eggs, and grow the eggs into soldiers, and Daniel is losing, because gathering is a coin-flip d6 and a run of bad rolls strands the entire strategy. That is complaint one. Complaint two is the gathering rules themselves, which ask players to *agree* whether a square could reasonably contain wood. In a competitive game he wants letters printed in the corners.

Everything else is enthusiasm. A machine in his home cave, repaired, now teleports items directly to him. A neutral quackalope wanders the board on a d6 laying eggs that function as grenades. The AI always moves toward whichever units moved, so keeping a squad still becomes a way to steer it. Eight factions across base and expansions, hero-only play for anyone who wants to control exactly one unit, and mix-and-match sides for solo games.

Point four is the art, and it earns the best line in the video: Lemon's monsters are somehow both grotesque and compassionate. This world, Daniel suspects, is full of pain.

----

The AI here chases whatever moved last, which makes standing still a tactic. Is exploitable AI a flaw in a solo game, or part of the puzzle?
